overview: The file brings together State Department material on Japanese transportation and military mobility between 1940 and 1942. It includes an October 1941 intelligence radiogram reporting new airfields and Japanese aircraft deployments in French Indochina, a cross-reference to information about supposed Japanese landing fields in Peru, and a March 1940 memorandum on Japan’s effort to achieve automotive self-sufficiency through Nissan and Toyoda while restricting Ford and General Motors. Collectively, the documents connect aviation intelligence, suspected overseas infrastructure, wartime industrial policy, and pressure on American-owned businesses.

subfiles.title: Radiogram on new airfields and Japanese aircraft in French Indochina
subfiles.to: War Department and listed U.S. defense and intelligence offices
subfiles.about: Reports two new airfields and the disposition of seventy-four Japanese military aircraft in French Indochina.
subfiles.summary: British intelligence reported new airfields at Takeo and Kampong Thom. Japanese air strength was listed as fighter and light-bomber squadrons at Hanoi and Tourane and mixed heavy- and light-bomber units at Saigon, totaling seventy-four aircraft. The radiogram was filed in Singapore on October 23 and recorded by the War Department on October 25, 1941, for wide defense and intelligence distribution.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to alleged Japanese landing fields in Peru
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a letter concerning supposed Japanese landing fields under construction in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references information about alleged Japanese landing fields being built in Peru. It identifies the source as a May 16, 1942 letter from the Justice Department associated with Hoover and directs the reader to file 894.20223/133.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japan’s automobile industry and pressure on Ford
subfiles.to: Mr. Hollingsch, according to an OCR-uncertain routing stamp
subfiles.about: Assesses Japanese truck production, restrictions on American automobile companies, and negotiations for a Ford-Nissan-Toyoda enterprise.
subfiles.summary: Drawing on a February 23 report and despatch by Consul Richard F. Boyce, the memorandum states that Nissan and Toyoda each produced about 15,000 trucks annually with strong army support, sufficient for Japan’s normal needs and potentially those of Manchukuo. It describes the vehicles as copied or adapted from American models, competently manufactured but made from inferior materials, and presents the industry as part of a drive for independence from the United States. Japanese authorities had sharply curtailed import permits for Ford and General Motors and were pressuring the firms to sell or reorganize; one proposal envisioned a new 50,000-unit company owned 40 percent by Ford and 30 percent each by Nissan and Toyoda. The concluding comment suggests the restrictions may have been bargaining pressure rather than proof that the Japanese army was ready to abandon American trucks.

interest: The file is useful because it juxtaposes operational intelligence on Japanese air power with economic intelligence about the industrial foundations of Japanese mobility. The detailed squadron counts and airfield coordinates provide a snapshot of the southward Japanese military buildup shortly before the Pacific War, while the automobile memorandum records Japanese efforts to reduce dependence on American technology and capital. The Peru cross-reference also illustrates how reports of possible Japanese aviation infrastructure in the Western Hemisphere circulated through State and Justice Department filing systems. Its apparently miscellaneous contents reveal both the breadth of the decimal-file transportation category and the administrative pathways by which military, diplomatic, and commercial intelligence were connected.
